reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / WHO Classification of Eye Tumours
clinicalPearls: An umbrella term for a spectrum of squamous dysplasia of the conjunctiva and cornea, ranging from mild intraepithelial dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma
Typically arises at the limbus within the interpalpebral fissure, presenting as a gelatinous, papilliform, or leukoplakic lesion often with prominent feeder vessels
Major risk factors are ultraviolet exposure, older age, fair skin, human papillomavirus, and immunosuppression including HIV, which drives more aggressive disease in younger patients
The disease progresses along a continuum from intraepithelial dysplasia through carcinoma in situ to frankly invasive squamous cell carcinoma breaching the basement membrane
Rose bengal or lissamine green staining and anterior-segment optical coherence tomography aid non-invasive assessment, but histology confirms the diagnosis and invasion status
Treatment options include complete surgical excision with a no-touch technique and adjunctive cryotherapy, or medical therapy with topical chemotherapy or interferon
Wide margins and cryotherapy to the surgical edges reduce recurrence, and diffuse or recurrent disease may be managed medically
reference.pathophysiology: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia encompasses a continuum of squamous epithelial dysplasia of the conjunctiva and cornea. Chronic ultraviolet damage, alongside cofactors such as human papillomavirus infection, immunosuppression, and older age, induces mutations in limbal epithelial stem cells, the presumed cells of origin at the interpalpebral limbus. Disordered proliferation begins as partial-thickness dysplasia, advances to full-thickness carcinoma in situ while the basement membrane remains intact, and, if the basement membrane is breached, becomes invasive squamous cell carcinoma with potential for deeper ocular and, less commonly, regional spread. The intraepithelial phases are typically indolent and amenable to topical therapy, whereas invasion signifies a more serious tumour requiring definitive surgical management.
additionalDifferentials: Conjunctival melanoma or primary acquired melanosis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting limbal location, feeder vessels, and leukoplakia
Vital-dye staining (rose bengal or lissamine green) to highlight abnormal epithelium
Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography showing thickened hyper-reflective epithelium with an abrupt transition
Impression cytology or incisional/excisional biopsy for histological confirmation
Assessment of invasion depth and margins on histopathology
Evaluation of immune status including HIV testing in aggressive or young-onset disease
redFlags: Fixation of the lesion to underlying sclera or intraocular extension suggesting invasive carcinoma
Rapidly enlarging or recurrent lesion despite treatment
Aggressive disease in a young or immunosuppressed patient prompting HIV testing
reference.prognosis: Most intraepithelial disease is controlled with complete excision or topical therapy and carries an excellent prognosis, though recurrence is not uncommon after narrow-margin surgery; invasive squamous cell carcinoma has a more guarded outlook with risk of ocular invasion and, rarely, regional or distant spread.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesion for a pterygium and excising it without histology, missing dysplasia or invasion
Performing narrow-margin excision without adjunctive cryotherapy, increasing recurrence
Failing to test for immunosuppression in aggressive or young-onset cases
Assuming intraepithelial disease when unrecognised invasion is present
management: Complete surgical excision with wide margins using a no-touch technique, with adjunctive conjunctival cryotherapy and corneal alcohol epitheliectomy
Topical medical therapy with interferon alfa-2b, mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil as primary treatment or as an adjuvant for diffuse disease or involved margins
For invasive squamous cell carcinoma, wider excision with adjuvant plaque brachytherapy or radiotherapy, escalating to enucleation or exenteration for extensive ocular invasion
Lifelong ultraviolet protection with sunglasses and avoidance of further solar exposure
Assessment and treatment of immunosuppression, including HIV testing in aggressive or young-onset disease
Long-term slit-lamp surveillance for recurrence, which is common after narrow-margin surgery
Referral to an ophthalmic oncology service for multidisciplinary management
